name: Emeka Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and run a solar-panel laminator in a factory. I finished secondary school and am still junior; the lead checks the first panel for trapped air after I change the film roll. I use an AI assistant every day to compare fault notes and explain heat settings, then check the panel under the lamp. The high operator rate gives our household room: my wife and I have two school-age children, a mortgage and ten months of expenses saved. Plenty of similar factory jobs are nearby. I enjoy teaching my children how a plain sheet becomes a working panel, but a ruined batch still stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the line that AI can shorten a handover, but the first panel still needs a lamp check. A neat fault note cannot pull a bubble out of a finished solar panel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The laminator keeps paying a higher rate and our ten-month reserve gives us room. There are many other factories nearby; I can keep learning this machine without a sudden change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep loading film and checking the first laminated panel with the lead. I would put a new fixed amount from each full pay packet into the household reserve after mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about continuing work. A small AI helper earns its place only when the physical panel passes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the lamp reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trapped air pocket appears as a pale circle near the cell edge. I mark the panel and stop the run before another rack is sealed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to ten months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife and I want to keep options for the children. The next transfer would be new wages, not the cash already in the reserve.

A **daily** AI fault note helps only if the real panel passes.
think: **Higher** pay and ten months saved secure our household in this mild case.
**Plenty** of nearby plants give us alternatives.
do: **Keep** loading laminator film and inspecting first panels with lead.
**Save** new money from full wages after family bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can schedule film deliveries and quality reports faster, while the laminator still needs a safe first-panel check. I would ask for paid practice on a new AI bubble-detection control before it reaches live production.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office work may shrink first. My current laminator shifts look secure, but an alert could tempt management to shorten paid inspection time and rush the junior operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid line shifts and ask the lead for a supervised stopped-line slot. If the plant offers it, I would learn the new AI detection controls, compare twenty marked panels with the lamp and keep the human check if the system misses an air pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a faster target, although our household wage looks safe for now. I would rather learn the new AI bubble control on paid time than argue over a ruined solar panel later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare the panels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark the air pockets seen under the lamp, then see whether the new control flags the same twenty panels. A missed bubble would keep that batch on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the fault helper I already know and decline the new control for now. The factory should pay for practice on its own line.

The **lamp** check remains on the clock during faster scheduling.
think: My **laminator** wage looks secure for now on the laminator.
**Rushed** inspection could create quality errors before robots change the line.
do: **Keep** paid shifts and first-panel lamp checks.
**Learn** new AI bubble detector in offered paid supervised stopped-line slot.
feel: **Uneasy** about faster targets with current pay secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team thinking AI reaches schedules in 2028 when I am forty-five, then capable hands-on robots reach panel loading around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A robot could feed film and clear panels with fewer junior operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose many paid loading hours once that equipment works. Ten months saved and plenty of nearby plants buy us search time, but the next operator job may not match my higher wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and ask for a fully funded electrical-test course on paid time with safe isolated-panel practice. If a posted nearby testing job accepts the qualification and pays our mortgage and bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; if hours fall first, I would apply to posted nearby laminator jobs at adequate pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic wage cut, though we have a reserve and actual workplaces to ask. I will not trade my solar-panel laminator wage for an unposted job promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the test course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified tester would show me how to isolate a panel, measure its output and record a fault safely. My secondary schooling and junior laminator work are not a testing qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another operator role worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting must name paid hours and a wage that covers mortgage, food and travel. I would compare that with our real budget before leaving this shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches schedules in 2031 when I am forty-eight, with capable panel robots around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five years is time to learn testing properly while the laminator still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect some loading hours to go, but a longer runway lets the reserve grow. A test certificate helps only if a nearby employer posts a role that pays for family life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid laminator job and add fresh money from each full wage to our reserve after bills. If a fully funded electrical-test course offers paid safe bench practice and a posted nearby role pays our mortgage, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; I would not leave on a course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about later shifts, but able to work toward a real qualification. Five years lets me measure whether the job market values it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does safe bench practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would isolate a test panel, measure voltage with a qualified technician beside me and record the result. A video alone would not make me safe with a live circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no testing post is advertised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning on the laminator and check other actual nearby factory postings. I would not spend our reserve on a certificate without work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches schedules in 2036 when I am fifty-three, and capable panel robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. Ten years lets us prepare while the current line still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be older, yet I will still need wages after fifty-six. Our reserve is strong, but I do not call it a retirement plan or a promise of another high-paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the laminator and save a new amount from every full pay packet. If offered paid safe practice, I would learn a new AI panel-diagnosis control beyond my current fault summaries; if a funded paid-time test course and posted nearby bill-covering role exist, I would qualify and apply after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant robot loading, though I have years to make real choices. I would rather keep the paid solar-panel shift than guess what a future loading robot will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new AI diagnosis add?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would compare heat and output patterns across panels and suggest a physical test, rather than only summarising a fault note. I would verify it on an isolated panel with a technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a machine of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have savings, but a machine purchase could put the mortgage at risk. I would choose paid training tied to a real job before spending family capital.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because panel-loading robots around 2031 could cut my higher-paid shifts while the mortgage remains. Paid electrical-test training and a posted nearby job at adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets a paid place to learn the next panel machine. My children see me use AI every day, but they also see me check a real panel before I say it works. A finished solar panel can look fine and still fail its electrical test.

headlineQuote: A finished solar panel can look fine and still fail its electrical test.
portrait: **Emeka**, forty-three, is a junior solar-panel laminator operator with secondary schooling and two school-age children.
He **uses** AI daily but checks actual panels under a lamp with the lead.
His **higher** pay, ten-month reserve and many nearby plants give financial room while a mortgage remains.
He **learns** new controls early and pursues funded paid testing training only with a posted adequate nearby job.
biggestWorry: **Fast** panel-handling robots around 2031 could cut Emeka’s higher-paid loading shifts.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** safe electrical-test training and a posted nearby job covering mortgage and bills would help.
